Luidia sarsii exhibits a notably high maximum reproductive output when maintained under stable conditions. At a water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], a single gravid adult can produce approximately 410 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 410 eggs per day], sustained over the course of the breeding season. This rate translates to a total annual fecundity in the hundreds of thousands, reflecting a life-history strategy that relies on the broadcast spawning of vast numbers of planktotrophic larvae. The wet weight at birth is a mere 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 0.8 mm; this minute size is typical of echinoderms that produce feeding larvae, as the small initial mass allows for a high fecundity per spawning event. The bipinnaria larva that emerges must undergo a prolonged planktonic phase before it can settle and metamorphose into a juvenile starfish, a process that is highly dependent on local food availability and thermal conditions.

The larval-juvenile transition in this species occurs after a distinct period of planktonic development. At 14 °C [T = 14 °C], metamorphosis is achieved approximately 46 days after hatching , a duration that aligns with estimates for other members of the family Luidiidae. Upon completion of metamorphic climax, the newly settled individual possesses a diameter at metamorphosis of 0.5 centimeters ; this dimension, though small, marks the onset of a benthic existence and the beginning of active predatory behavior on small infaunal organisms. The transition from a free-swimming larval form to a crawling juvenile involves a dramatic body plan reorganisation, including the resorption of larval arms and the development of the adult rudiment. This morphological transformation is energetically demanding, and juveniles that settle in areas with low prey density often fail to thrive, a bottleneck that can shape local population dynamics.

As the post-metamorphic juvenile enters its sub-adult phase, growth proceeds steadily, and sexual maturation begins after a specific interval from birth. At 14 °C [T = 14 °C], puberty is attained 365 days after hatching [tp = 365 days after hatching], meaning that individuals born in one spawning season become reproductively competent by the following year. This relatively rapid maturation is consistent with the species' role as a generalist predator in subtidal soft-bottom habitats, where high turnover and early reproduction can offset the considerable mortality experienced during the planktonic larval stage. The onset of gametogenesis is triggered by a combination of photoperiod and thermal cues, ensuring that spawning coincides with periods of peak phytoplankton abundance for the feeding larvae. Reaching this developmental milestone at approximately one year of age allows the species to maintain robust population densities even in environments subject to frequent physical disturbance.

Feeding experiments conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have clarified the trophic energetics of this sea star. In trials where individuals of 8.93 grams wet body mass were offered brittle stars, the average feeding rate recorded at 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C] was 0.587 grams per day . This value was derived from observations showing that over a 21-day period, a group of ten sea stars consumed a total of 28.4 brittle stars each weighing 0.434 grams. The corresponding gain in wet body mass for these individuals was 3.8 grams over the same interval, yielding a growth rate of 0.158 grams per day  when calculated across the entire feeding period at a temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C]. This relationship between ingestion and somatic increase suggests that a substantial fraction of the assimilated energy is directed into structural growth rather than being expended solely on metabolic demands, a pattern that is typical for active foragers with relatively high food conversion efficiencies.

Maximum recorded longevity for Luidia sarsii is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] when animals are maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], though field-based estimates suggest that few individuals in natural populations reach this upper limit due to the cumulative impacts of predation and incidental capture in trawling gear. The ultimate radius attained by the largest specimens is 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size that grants adults access to larger prey items, including ophiuroids and small bivalves, which are more energetically profitable than the smaller infauna consumed by juveniles. This combination of a moderate lifespan and a fairly large adult body size places Luidia sarsii at the slower end of the fast-slow continuum for temperate asteroids. The species thus balances the high fecundity characteristic of free-spawning marine invertebrates with a growth trajectory that allows it to dominate the predator guild in its preferred soft-sediment habitats.
